item.text:
**5B.6 Research Note: Sheikh Hasina in 2024**
Overall judgment: **mixed, leaning yes on visible investment effort, but uneven and not fully durable**. Bangladesh did put real money and administrative effort into infrastructure, procurement digitization, health-system planning, and some climate-resilient public works. But education continuity, regulatory predictability, and the broader investment climate remained weak.

**Accepted Claims**

- [Bangladesh receives $900 million World Bank financing to increase economic and urban resilience for sustainable growth](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/06/21/bangladesh-receives-900-million-world-bank-financing-to-increase-economic-and-urban-resilience-for-sustainable-growth) | World Bank | June 21, 2024 | The Bank described support for fiscal and financial-sector reforms plus climate-resilient urban management, including better roads, bus terminals, and city-cluster infrastructure to strengthen competitiveness and public services. This is strong evidence that the government was investing in infrastructure and predictable policy foundations for productivity. `Question IDs: 5B.6, 5B.4, 5B.3`

- [World Bank helps Bangladesh Develop Bay Terminal](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/06/28/world-bank-helps-bangladesh-develop-bay-terminal) | World Bank | June 28, 2024 | The Bay Terminal project was framed as a trade-competitiveness investment that would reduce import/export costs, improve port efficiency, and mobilize private investment. This is direct evidence of infrastructure investment aimed at long-run productivity and trade capacity. `Question IDs: 5B.6, 5B.4`

- [Inclusion of govt procuring agencies in e-GP mandatory](https://bppa.gov.bd/media-communication/news-1446.html) | Bangladesh Public Procurement Authority | March 6, 2024 | The BPPA said e-GP was mandatory for government agencies, with most agencies already registered, and that online procurement had improved transparency, efficiency, and competition. This is strong evidence of administrative capacity-building and more predictable procurement rules. `Question IDs: 5B.6, 5B.4, 5B.5`

- [Advancing Healthcare Excellence: WHO's Role in Developing the First National Medical Education Strategy in Bangladesh!](https://www.who.int/bangladesh/news/detail/04-03-2024-advancing-healthcare-excellence-who-s-role-in-developing-the-first-national-medical-education-strategy-in-bangladesh) | WHO Bangladesh | March 4, 2024 | The health ministry, with WHO support, launched work on Bangladesh’s first national medical education strategy to improve curriculum, accreditation, faculty development, and digital transformation. This is direct evidence of investment in health workforce quality and education foundations. `Question IDs: 5B.6`

- [Bangladesh completes its second Joint External Evaluation of the International Health Regulations core capacities](https://www.who.int/southeastasia/news/detail/11-07-2024-2nd-jee-bn) | WHO | July 11, 2024 | Bangladesh completed its second JEE using the new eJEE platform, reviewing core health-security capacities and recommending priority actions. This is a real signal of administrative and technical capacity-building, though it is narrower than broad education or infrastructure policy. `Question IDs: 5B.6, 5B.2`

- [Bangladesh Receives $900 Million World Bank Financing to Improve Environment Sustainability, Urban and Climate Resilience](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/12/23/bangladesh-receives-900-million-world-bank-financing-to-improve-environment-sustainability-urban-and-climate-resilience) | World Bank | December 22, 2024 | The financing package included climate-resilient urban infrastructure, roads, bus terminals, markets, parks, toilets, and bridges, plus planning and financing reforms. This is strong evidence of late-2024 investment in physical infrastructure and state planning capacity. `Question IDs: 5B.6, 5B.4`

- [The World Bank In Bangladesh 2024](https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099514001022413953) | World Bank | December 31, 2023 / disclosed January 2, 2024 | The report highlighted Bangladesh’s long-run gains in gender parity in school enrollment and large reductions in maternal and child mortality. This is positive background evidence that the state already had some human-capital and health-capacity foundations entering 2024. `Question IDs: 5B.6`

**Counterevidence**

- [Financial Sector and Fiscal Policy Reforms Will Help Bangladesh Sustain Strong Growth](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/04/02/financial-sector-and-fiscal-policy-reforms-will-help-bangladesh-sustain-strong-growth-despite-strong-growth-south-asia-r) | World Bank | April 2, 2024 | The Bank said growth was being disrupted by high inflation, a balance-of-payments deficit, financial-sector vulnerabilities, tight liquidity, import restrictions, and higher input costs that dampened investment. This undercuts any claim that the productivity foundations were already operating smoothly. `Question IDs: 5B.6, 5B.3`

- [Bold and Timely Reforms will Help Bangladesh Create Quality Jobs and Achieve Inclusive Growth](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/10/15/bold-and-timely-reforms-will-help-bangladesh-create-quality-jobs-and-achieve-inclusive-growth-world-bank) | World Bank | October 15, 2024 | The World Bank said inflation, balance-of-payments pressure, financial vulnerabilities, and subdued investment were still limiting jobs, especially for youth and educated workers. That points to a productivity agenda that was still incomplete and under strain. `Question IDs: 5B.6, 5B.3`

- [Bangladesh Development Update - Special Focus: Creating Jobs for a Better Future](https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099104310142425439) | World Bank | October 1, 2024 | The report said SMEs faced high regulatory costs, unreliable infrastructure, and limited finance, and it called for stronger competition policy and competitive neutrality for state-owned enterprises. This is strong evidence that predictable, productivity-enhancing rules were still missing. `Question IDs: 5B.6, 5B.4, 5B.5`

- [35 million children in Bangladesh had schooling disrupted by Climate Crises in 2024](https://www.unicef.org/bangladesh/en/press-releases/33-million-children-bangladesh-had-schooling-disrupted-climate-crises-2024unicef) | UNICEF | January 24, 2025 | UNICEF reported that climate hazards disrupted schooling for 35 million children in Bangladesh during 2024, including closures from heatwaves, cyclones, and floods. That is strong negative evidence for continuity in the education foundation, even though it is a 2025 report about 2024. `Question IDs: 5B.6`

**Bottom Line**
Hasina’s government did make real 2024 investments in infrastructure, procurement digitization, health-system planning, and climate-resilient public works. But the broader productivity foundation was still fragile: education was repeatedly disrupted, investment remained subdued, and the regulatory/infrastructure environment for firms and jobs was still weak.

**Search gap**
I did not find strong 2024 evidence that Hasina personally delivered a broad, across-the-board improvement in education quality or regulatory predictability. The best positives are sectoral and project-specific; the negatives show the system was still operating under major macro, climate, and administrative constraints.
